extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, judges, and law students (practitioners of patent-transfer law)
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and substantive standards governing the transfer (assignment, sale, recording) of patents and patent rights, including warranties, notice/recording effects, the relation of legal and equitable title, and estoppel. Focused on how assignments affect enforcement rights and third-party purchasers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment carries rights of action for past infringements
rubrics_metrics.description: Unless so expressed, an assignment carries rights of action for past infringements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where an assignment transfers the patent right it ordinarily includes the right to sue for past infringements unless the assignment expressly excludes that right. Exception: an assignment by an administrator under a court order does not carry the right of action for past infringements (cases cited: May v. Juneau Co.; McCullough (1858); Fisher).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment of an undivided part creates joint ownership
rubrics_metrics.description: The assignment of an undivided part of the entire interest creates a joint ownership in the invention and the monopoly, the proportion of each co-owner being determined by the provisions of the assignment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Co-owners' relations and rights to enjoyment/partition/licensing are governed by the assignment terms and by separate principles applicable to co-owners; these rights are treated elsewhere in the treatise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implied warranty of title from assignment for valuable consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: From the assignment of a patented invention for a valuable consideration a warranty of title to it, and of a right to assign it according to the terms of the assignment, is implied by law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The implied warranty grows out of the sale itself (not the form of the conveyance). It draws after any subsequently acquired title of the assignor necessary to make the transfer valid. Express covenants of warranty may be inserted and may wholly or partially supersede the implied warranty. The assignee may recover damages for breach of warranty (see §§1229–1232). A sale of a patent right that includes agreement to protect vendee from suits for infringement on other patents is a warranty that the article does not infringe other patents (Croningw. Paige).

rubrics_metrics.name: No implied warranty of patent validity in bona fide exchanges
rubrics_metrics.description: There is doubt whether there is any implied warranty of validity in the sale of a patent where all is done in good faith and both parties are equally ignorant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases are cited indicating that where both parties are equally ignorant in good faith, a warranty that the patent is valid may not be implied (Hiatt v. Twomey). The purchaser who pays nothing or only signs as inducement (e.g., subscriber) runs his own risk and does not warrant validity or value (Llane v. Smith).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sale of a patent revokes revocable licenses and terminates powers of attorney
rubrics_metrics.description: The conveyance of a patent revokes all revocable licenses; the sale of a patent terminates prior powers of attorney.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited cases: Shaw v. Colwell Lead Co. (revocable licenses), Labaree v. Peoria, Pekin & Jacksonville R.R. Co. (termination of powers of attorney). Assignees who allow a power of attorney to remain and permit others to act may be bound by it (Labaree).

rubrics_metrics.name: Secret licensing or fraud in relation to assignment defeats rights
rubrics_metrics.description: If a patentee sells a patent (e.g., to a corporation) and, having secured an assignment for extension, secretly licenses to others before signing back to the corporation, it is a fraud on the corporation and the licensee acquires no rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example case: Consolidated Fruit Jar Co. v. Mason. Secret licenses or transfers intended to deceive the grantee will be treated as fraudulent and not effective against the transferee.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment of an expired patent limited to power to collect past damages
rubrics_metrics.description: The assignment of an expired patent may be good as a power of attorney to collect damages for past infringements, but not otherwise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An expired patent cannot generally be assigned as a continuing right; at most an assignment of an expired patent may serve as a power to collect past damages (BeQ v. McCullough (1858); Fisher).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recording requirement: assignments must be recorded within three months
rubrics_metrics.description: An assignment shall be recorded in the Patent Office within three months after the date of its execution; failure to record within three months renders the prior conveyance invalid as against subsequent purchasers or mortgagees for value without notice, except where actual notice exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: During the three-month window a subsequent alienee must investigate and runs the risk of defective title. After three months an unrecorded prior assignment is invalid against later transfers (Sec. 4898 Rev. Stat., cases: Tumbull v. Weir Plow Co.; Gibson v. Cook). The record of the title in the Patent Office is conclusive in favor of bona fide purchasers with no other knowledge beyond the record. The assignee of record may rely on the record title (e.g., Campbell v. James).

rubrics_metrics.name: Record is constructive notice to the world; effect on third parties and Commissioner
rubrics_metrics.description: The record of assignments and patents in the Patent Office furnishes constructive notice to all the world and is conclusive in favor of bona fide purchasers who have no other knowledge of the title.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After record (and after the three-month period has elapsed) the record affords constructive notice to all persons acquiring interests subsequently to the date of record. The Commissioner must be governed by the record title and cannot regard mere equitable claims (Ex parte Edison). The record is chargeable with such knowledge as a search of the records would convey (National Car Brake Shoe Co. v. Terre Haute Car & Mfg. Co.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Record of only certain instruments is constructive notice; unrecordable instruments not notice
rubrics_metrics.description: The law provides for recording only three instruments: an assignment before patent when the patent is to issue to the assignee (alone or jointly), an assignment after patent, and a grant. The record of no other instrument than these affords constructive notice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if other documents are placed on record, they do not create constructive notice under the statute. They may, however, be actual notice to particular persons. Examples and cases: Sec. 4895 Rev. Stat.; Wright v. Bandel; Perry v. Corning; Brooks v. Byam.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment before patent must include request for issue to assignee to secure priority
rubrics_metrics.description: An assignment made before patent issue, unaccompanied by a request that the patent issue to the assignee, cannot prevail over a subsequent assignment that contains such a request to a bona fide assignee for value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under the statutes and cases, to secure the patent to an assignee of record when the assignment is before issue, the proper request must accompany the assignment; otherwise a later bona fide assignee who requests issue to him and records properly may obtain the patent (Wright v. Bandel; United States Stamping Co. v. Jewett).

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of legal and equitable title; effects and equity remedies
rubrics_metrics.description: Legal and equitable titles to a patented invention may become separated and vest in different owners; an assignment before grant creates an equitable title in the assignee while legal title may remain in the inventor until issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where legal and equitable titles are severed, a court of equity will treat the holder of legal title as trustee for equitable owner and compel conveyances or other acts to protect equitable rights. If legal and equitable titles unite in same person they prevail over other mere equitable titles unless the legal owner had notice of the equities (cases: Aspinwall Mfg. Co. v. Gill; Davis Wagon Wheel Co. v. Davis Wagon Co.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignee cannot sue on patent until assignment recorded (in some jurisdictions)
rubrics_metrics.description: An assignment must be recorded before the assignee can sue on the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case example: Wyeth v. Stone (1840) — recording requirement as a condition precedent to assignee's right to sue has been held in certain cases. Parties are advised to record promptly to preserve enforcement rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record of assignment of a right of action is not constructive notice to the party sued
rubrics_metrics.description: The record of an assignment of a right of action under a patent is not constructive notice to the party against whom such action lies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although the record may give notice to purchasers generally, a record of assignment of the right of action does not operate as constructive notice to the defendant sued on that right (treatise note).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignee of record who takes with notice of prior unrecorded conveyances acquires at most legal title
rubrics_metrics.description: An assignee of record, taking his assignment with notice of prior unrecorded conveyances, acquires at most the legal title only, while the equitable title remains in the prior alienee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recording an assignment with notice of prior equities does not wipe out earlier equitable rights; the prior unrecorded equitable owner may enforce equitable rights in chancery. Cases: Aspinwall Mfg. Co., Wright v. Bandel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estoppel of assignor and parties who accept benefits of assignment
rubrics_metrics.description: The assignor of a patented invention is estopped from denying the validity of the patent or his own title to the interest transferred. Parties subsequently becoming interested with the assignee and who accept benefits are likewise bound by the same estoppel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estoppel operates even where the patent is invalid or title void as against the world, insofar as the assignor has conveyed and the assignee (or transferees accepting benefits) relies on that conveyance (cases: American Paper Barrel Co. v. Laraway; Time Telegraph Co. v. Carey). If an assignee repudiates and relinquishes benefits, the estoppel may cease to operate. Estoppel prevents the assignor (or one who takes benefits) from defending against obligations (e.g., royalties) by asserting invalidity/fraud in the assignor unless the assignee has renounced benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignee who enjoys benefits cannot avoid obligations by asserting patent invalidity
rubrics_metrics.description: Where by the terms of the assignment the assignee becomes liable for royalties or shares in profits, he cannot in an account action defend on the ground that the invention was unpatentable or the patent void if he has received and continues to enjoy the benefits of the assignment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the assignee discovers defects and repudiates the assignment and relinquishes benefits, estoppel may end. Example cases: Shaw v. Soule; Kinsman v. Parkhurst; where assignee manufactured under the patent terms they could not deny validity when called to account.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parol warranty cannot be set up if conveyance contains no warranty
rubrics_metrics.description: If the instrument conveying the patent contains no warranty, the vendee cannot set up a parol warranty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where the conveyance is silent as to warranty, extrinsic (parol) warranties will not be read in to alter the recorded instrument (Joliffe v. Collins). Parties should include express covenants if they intend warranty protection beyond implied law.
